title: Uterine Rupture
subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: A full‑thickness tear of the uterine wall, usually in a scarred or over‑distended uterus, causing fetal and maternal compromise. Rapid recognition and surgical repair are life‑saving.

sections.p: Uterine rupture is a complete disruption of the uterine wall, often through a previous scar or over‑distension. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by fetal heart tracing and, if available, ultrasound or CT.

t.b: Loss of variability or bradycardia indicates fetal distress
Shows discontinuity of myometrium, free fluid in abdomen

sections.p: Staging follows the WHO classification: Type I (incomplete), Type II (complete but uterus intact), Type III (complete with uterine rupture).
b: Type III – complete tear, uterus ruptures into abdomen

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, the leading causes are obstructed labour, previous caesarean scar, grand multiparity, and excessive uterine stimulation.
b: Malaria or HIV‑related anaemia increasing risk of uterine over‑distension

sections.p: Sudden, severe abdominal pain, loss of fetal station, abnormal CTG, vaginal bleeding, and signs of haemodynamic instability.
Use bedside tests; when unavailable, rely on clinical signs.

t.b: Detects fetal distress; loss of variability suggests uterine rupture
Shows free fluid and discontinuity of myometrium; if not available, look for abdominal distension and tenderness
Drop indicates blood loss; <7 g/dL is a red flag

sections.p: Immediate maternal and fetal death, massive haemorrhage, sepsis, uterine inversion, and peritonitis.
b: Peritonitis – from spillage of amniotic fluid

sections.p: Urgent surgical exploration, control bleeding, repair uterus or perform hysterectomy if needed, and supportive care.
b: Monitor fetal heart and maternal vitals continuously

sections.p: Post‑operative monitoring for infection, haemorrhage, and future pregnancy planning. Prevention focuses on timely referral, safe induction practices, and scar assessment.
b: Plan for caesarean if scarred uterus

sections.p: Placental abruption, uterine inversion, and severe postpartum haemorrhage.
b: Post‑partum haemorrhage – often from atony, not wall rupture

sections.p: Normal CTG can mask rupture if fetal monitoring is intermittent; ultrasound may miss a small tear.
b: Hemoglobin may remain normal early if bleeding is slow

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain during labour
Vaginal bleeding or gush of blood

faq.q: What is the most common risk factor for uterine rupture in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Previous caesarean scar or other uterine surgery, especially when labour is prolonged or obstructed.

faq.q: Why is oxytocin avoided after a uterine rupture?
faq.a: It can increase uterine tone and worsen bleeding or re‑rupture the repaired wall.

faq.q: Can a uterine rupture be diagnosed with a bedside ultrasound?
faq.a: Yes, it can show free fluid and discontinuity of the myometrium, but clinical signs are paramount if imaging is unavailable.

exam: A woman in labour with a previous caesarean presents with sudden abdominal pain and loss of fetal station — what is your next step? — Immediate laparotomy after confirming fetal distress on CTG.
You suspect uterine rupture but the CTG is normal; what should you do? — Repeat CTG and perform bedside ultrasound; if unavailable, observe for haemodynamic changes.
A patient has a uterine rupture and is haemodynamically unstable; which drug is contraindicated? — Oxytocin, as it may worsen bleeding.
During repair, you notice a 2‑cm tear in the lower uterine segment; how do you suture? — Layer‑by‑layer interrupted sutures with non‑absorbable material.
Post‑repair, the patient develops fever and abdominal pain; what complication is likely? — Peritonitis from spillage of amniotic fluid.
A woman with a known uterine scar is in labour; what induction agent should you avoid? — High‑dose oxytocin or misoprostol without careful monitoring.
